question: A 25-year-old man who lives in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia attends your clinic complaining of a progressive skin eruption of the body and limbs for 1 year. The rash is not itchy or painful.  He has had no previous skin problems and no contact with a similarly affected person. His appearance gradually changed over 12 months. There is a papular and nodular eruption on the extensor aspects of the forearms, arms, thighs and trunk. Furthermore, there is a diffuse infiltration of the skin of the face and nodules on the pinnae, with madarosis (loss of eyebrows and eyelashes). There is no loss of sensation within the skin lesions and no sensory or motor loss in the hands or feet. What is the most likely diagnosis?

retrieved_contexts.Title: An 18-Year-Old Man from India With a Pale Patch on His Right Upper Limb
retrieved_contexts.History: An 18-year-old man from India has noticed a pale patch on his right arm and forearm for 3 months. It is not itchy or painful, but he reports reduced sensation in the affected area. He also complains of mild numbness of the little finger of the right hand but no weakness (he is right-handed). Otherwise he is well. There is no family history of skin problems.
retrieved_contexts.Clinical_Findings: There is a 20 cm by 10 cm hypopigmented macule on the outer aspect of the right arm extending on to the forearm (Fig. 83.1). The affected skin is dry. The sensation within the hypopigmented area is reduced compared with the normally pigmented skin. The rest of the skin examination is normal. Both ulnar nerves are palpable, however the right ulnar nerve is thickened. There is reduced sensation on the tip and ulnar border of the right little finger. There are no other neurological abnormalities.
retrieved_contexts.Discussion: An 18-year-old man from India presents with a hypopigmented macular lesion on the right arm with reduced sensation. A hypopigmented anaesthetic patch is a cardinal sign of leprosy. The combination of a skin problem and signs of a neuropathy should always raise the suspicion of leprosy.

retrieved_contexts.Title: A 55-Year-Old Indigenous Woman from Australia With a Widespread Exfoliating Rash and Sepsis
retrieved_contexts.History: You are working in a remote indigenous community in tropical northern Australia, and the community health worker asks you to visit a house to assess an elderly woman who has been living in the crowded back room. Her family are worried that she has become increasingly withdrawn and hasn’t been getting out of the house much at all.
retrieved_contexts.Clinical_Findings: The patient is a 55-year-old indigenous Australian woman with a widespread exfoliative rash involving all limbs and especially the armpits, buttocks and thighs (Fig. 10.1). Many flakes of skin cover the mattress she is lying on. In addition, she has fissures over her wrists and knees. She also looks pale, is clammy and poorly responsive. Her temperature is 39.5°C (103.1°F), heart rate 110bpm, respiratory rate 28 breath cycles per minute and blood pressure 85mmHg systolic to radial pulsation. Oxygen saturation by pulse oximetry is 92% on room air.
retrieved_contexts.Discussion: A 55-year-old indigenous Australian woman has a widespread exfoliating rash and is clearly systemically unwell with signs of sepsis.

retrieved_contexts.Title: A 24-Year-Old Man from Malawi With Skin Lesions and Breathlessness
retrieved_contexts.History: A 24-year-old Malawian businessman presents to your clinic having noticed dark spots on his arm and leg for the last month. The lesions are progressing and he is now getting facial swelling. On questioning, he also reports a 3-month history of cough and worsening shortness of breath. He has no constitutional symptoms of weight loss, fevers or night sweats. His cough is productive of white sputum. He has no history of previous tuberculosis. He tested positive for HIV a week before coming to your clinic and has not yet started antiretroviral medication.
retrieved_contexts.Clinical_Findings: The patient appears comfortable at rest with moderate facial oedema (Fig. 59.1). His temperature is 36°C (96.8°F), respiratory rate 32 breath cycles per minute and pulse 102 bpm. Widespread dark-purplish plaques are noted on the skin (Fig. 59.1) and palate. On respiratory examination, he has decreased air entry and dullness at the right lung base. He has swelling of his right leg from the foot to the knee, with prominent dark plaques which are coalescing (Fig. 59.2). The rest of the physical examination is normal.
retrieved_contexts.Discussion: A young Malawian man presents with widespread dark purplish cutaneous and mucosal lesions. He also reports cough and shortness of breath for 3 months and there are some chest findings on examination of his right lung. He has recently been found to be HIV-positive. • Fig. 59.1 Facial swelling and dark-purplish skin lesions on chest and nose of the patient. • Fig. 59.2 Swollen right leg with prominent coalescing dark plaques. 162

retrieved_contexts.Title: A 7-Year-Old Girl from West Africa With Two Skin Ulcers and a Contracture of Her Right Wrist
retrieved_contexts.History: A 7-year-old girl is presented to a district hospital in the tropical region of a West African country. After an insect bite, she developed an itchy papule on the back of her right hand, which enlarged over a period of 3 months. A traditional healer had prescribed herbal remedies. When the lesion ulcerated a few weeks later, diclofenac and dexamethasone were administered at the local health post. When a second lesion appeared, treatment with oxacillin was initiated with no effect. The girl became increasingly unable to use her right hand. There is no history of relevant trauma or systemic symptoms.
retrieved_contexts.Clinical_Findings: A 7-year-old, anxious girl in good general condition holding her right wrist in a 45° flexion and 20° abduction position. Pulse 108bpm (normal 70–110), blood pressure 100/ 70mmHg, temperature 37.9°C (100.2°F). Two skin ulcers are present on the back of her right hand (3  3cm) and on the medial side of her right wrist (0.5  1cm). The larger ulcer is filled with necrotic tissue (Fig. 41.1) and surrounded by hypo- and hyperpigmentation, lichenification and desquamation. An ill-defined induration surrounds the ulcers (12  8cm) with oedema extending from the lower arm to the fingers. A 0.5  0.5cm nodule is noticed above the medial right elbow.
retrieved_contexts.Discussion: A 7-year-old West African girl presents with two progressive cutaneous ulcers linked by an area of altered skin. The movement in the associated joint is restricted. General symptoms are limited to a mildly elevated temperature.

retrieved_contexts.Title: A 7-Year-Old Girl from Peru With a Chronic Skin Ulcer
retrieved_contexts.History: A 7-year-old girl who lives in the Peruvian capital, Lima, is brought to a local clinic because of a chronic skin lesion on her nose. The lesion appeared 4 months ago as a small nodule and slowly turned into an ulcer. It is a bit itchy but not painful. There is no history of trauma. The girl is otherwise healthy. Six months ago, she travelled to a valley on the western slopes of the Andes.
retrieved_contexts.Clinical_Findings: The lesion is a localized ulcer on the nose (Fig. 2.1). The borders of the ulcer are indurated and there is a plaque-like infiltration of the surrounding skin. The whole lesion is about 2cm in diameter. There are no palpable lymph nodes. She is afebrile and the rest of the physical examination is normal.
retrieved_contexts.Discussion: A 7-year-old Peruvian girl presents with a painless ulcerative skin lesion on her nose, which has been present for the past 4 months. There are no systemic symptoms.

retrieved_contexts.Title: A 6-Year-Old Boy from Malawi With Fever, Cough and Impaired Consciousness
retrieved_contexts.History: You review a 6-year-old boy in the paediatric high dependency unit of a Malawian Central Hospital. The boy was admitted the night before because of high fever, dyspnoea and a dry cough which had started 3 days before. On admission, he was started on presumptive antimalarial treatment; the results of the malaria smear are pending. The boy is known to be HIV-positive but is not yet on antiretroviral therapy (ART).
retrieved_contexts.Clinical_Findings: Examination reveals a sick child with a temperature of 39.8°C (103.6°F) and laboured breathing. The Blantyre coma score is 3/5. The boy has coryza and bilateral conjunctivitis. Behind both ears and on the forehead, you notice a fine maculopapular rash that has not been described before. There is bilateral axillary lymphadenopathy.
retrieved_contexts.Discussion: An HIV-positive Malawian boy presents with high fever, dry cough, coryza, conjunctivitis and impaired level of consciousness together with a fine maculopapular rash on the neck and face.

retrieved_contexts.Title: A 72-Year-Old Male Farmer from Laos With Extensive Skin Lesions on the Lower Leg
retrieved_contexts.History: A 72-year-old male farmer is admitted to a provincial hospital in northern Laos with extensive, painful verrucous skin lesions on his left foot and lower leg. Ten years prior, he had a leech bite on the dorsum of his left foot. One week later a small painless red nodule developed at the site of the bite. Over the following years the lesion slowly increased in size; further lesions developed and spread up to his knee. Three days before admission his ankle became painful and swollen.
retrieved_contexts.Clinical_Findings: Vital signs are normal and the patient is afebrile. His left lower leg and foot are grossly swollen (Fig. 25.1); the skin is hyperaemic and feels hot. There are several cauliflower-like masses and oval plaque-like lesions on his left lower leg and foot. The lesions are partly erythematous, partly fungating and purulent, oozing a bad odour.
retrieved_contexts.Discussion: A male Lao farmer presents with several verrucous, partially fungating skin lesions on his left leg and foot, which have been growing over the past 10years after a minor trauma. The affected leg has additionally swollen up and become painful over the previous 3 days. • Fig. 25.1 Lower legs of the patient at presentation with fungating lesions on his left foot that spread centripetally up to his knee. The left lower leg is also swollen and hyperaemic. 67

retrieved_contexts.Title: A 20-Year-Old Woman from the Democratic Republic of the Congo With Fever and a Vesiculopustular Skin Rash
retrieved_contexts.History: A 20-year-old woman presents to her local hospital in a rural area of the Democratic Republic of the Congo with a history of fever, malaise, headache, dry cough, swelling of the neck and a disseminated skin rash, which appeared 2 days after the symptoms began. The skin lesions first appeared on the face and then spread centrifugally over her body, including the palms and soles of her feet as well as the oral mucosa. The lesions have developed from initial macules to papules, then to vesicles and finally to pustules. The oral mucosal lesions are painful and make drinking and eating difficult. The patient resides in a village, where people live from agriculture, she has no relevant past medical history and is the mother of three children.
retrieved_contexts.Clinical_Findings: Vital signs: temperature 38°C (100.4°F), pulse 110 beats per minute, blood pressure 105/82 mmHg. Disseminated uniform umbilicated vesiculopustular skin lesions, ranging from 0.5 to 1 cm in diameter, all over the body with a predilection for the face, the hands and the feet (Fig. 94.1). Generalized lymphadenopathy with prominent swelling of the cervical lymph nodes. The examination of the lungs, heart, abdomen and the CNS is unremarkable.
retrieved_contexts.Discussion: A 20-year-old woman from a rural region of the Democratic Republic of the Congo presents with an acute febrile illness which is accompanied by a disseminated uniform vesiculopustular skin rash including the palms and soles of the feet as well as the oral mucosa and a prominent cervical lymphadenopathy.

answer:
Disease: Diffuse Cutaneous Leishmaniasis (DCL); Reasoning: The patient's presentation aligns perfectly with DCL caused by *Leishmania aethiopica*, which is endemic in Ethiopia. The key features supporting this diagnosis are:
1. **Epidemiology:** Residence in an endemic region.
2. **Clinical Picture:** Chronic (1 year), progressive, widespread papulonodular eruption on the face and extensor surfaces.
3. **Specific Signs:** Diffuse facial infiltration, nodules on the pinnae, and madarosis are all characteristic.
4. **Decisive Negative Finding:** The complete absence of sensory loss within the lesions is the most crucial piece of evidence that distinguishes DCL from its main mimic, lepromatous leprosy. While Case 83 describes a different form of leprosy, it reinforces the importance of sensory loss in diagnosing that disease, and its absence here strongly points towards DCL.; Likelihood: high
Disease: Lepromatous Leprosy (LL); Reasoning: LL is the primary differential diagnosis due to the striking clinical similarity. The widespread, symmetrical papules, nodules, facial infiltration, and madarosis are classic features of LL. Leprosy is also endemic in Ethiopia. However, the diagnosis is significantly weakened by the complete absence of sensory loss in the lesions and lack of palpable, thickened peripheral nerves after one year of disease progression. As highlighted by the contrast with Case 83, neurological involvement is a cardinal sign of leprosy. While sensory loss can be late-onset in LL, its total absence makes this diagnosis less probable than DCL.; Likelihood: moderate
Disease: Post-Kala-Azar Dermal Leishmaniasis (PKDL); Reasoning: PKDL can present with skin lesions identical to DCL. It is also endemic in the region. However, this diagnosis is contingent on a previous episode of visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar), which typically involves a prolonged history of fever, weight loss, and hepatosplenomegaly. The patient's history lacks any such preceding illness, making PKDL unlikely. No retrieved cases are relevant to this diagnosis.; Likelihood: low
Disease: Cutaneous Sarcoidosis; Reasoning: Sarcoidosis is a multisystem granulomatous disease that can manifest with skin papules and nodules, which can mimic the patient's presentation. However, it is a diagnosis of exclusion and is far less common than infectious causes like leishmaniasis and leprosy in this epidemiological context. The absence of other systemic symptoms (e.g., respiratory) also makes it less likely. No retrieved cases are relevant to this diagnosis.; Likelihood: low

question: A 46-year-old male Swiss traveller spent a 2-week holiday in the border region of Argentine and Brazil. Two weeks after his return, he developed flu-like symptoms and exertional dyspnoea. Ten days after the onset of symptoms, the patient presented at his general practitioner with fever and a pronounced frontal headache.

retrieved_contexts.Title: A 51-Year-Old Female Traveller Returning from Central America With Conjunctivitis, Rash and Peripheral Oedema
retrieved_contexts.History: A 51-year-old female Swiss traveller presented to the outpatient department 6 days after returning from a 2-week holiday to Guatemala and El Salvador. Four days after her return, the patient noticed a generalized slightly pruritic maculopapular rash on the face, trunk, and extremities. There was no fever and no other accompanying symptoms. On the next day the rash worsened and a non-purulent bilateral conjunctivitis developed. The patient did not report any chronic underlying disease nor the intake of any medication.
retrieved_contexts.Clinical_Findings: The patient was afebrile. Upon inspection there was conjunctivitis and a generalised maculopapular rash, also involving the face. Additionally, the patient showed tender oedema of the hands, elbows, knees and feet (Fig. 77.1). There was also generalized lymphadenopathy (cervical, axillary, and inguinal).
retrieved_contexts.Discussion: Six days after returning from a 2-week holiday to Guatemala and El Salvador, a 51-year-old female Swiss traveller presents with a slightly pruritic disseminated maculopapular rash, conjunctivitis, peripheral painful oedema (hands, elbows, knees and feet) and a generalized lymphadenopathy.

retrieved_contexts.Title: A 36-Year-Old Male Traveller Returning from Botswana With a Creeping Eruption
retrieved_contexts.History: A 36-year-old male restaurant owner presents to a travel clinic in Europe with a mobile itchy mass under his skin. Three weeks ago, he noted the mass in his groin for 4 days after which it subsided. He then noted an itchy, serpiginous rash tracking from his groin to his chest, which moved over the course of several days and then disappeared; he then noted the mass reappearing on his right shoulder, at which point he was referred for assessment. There is no history of fever or systemic illness. Five weeks ago, he returned from a fishing holiday with four friends to the Okavango Delta in Botswana. He took malaria chemoprophylaxis, slept on the boat under a mosquito net and swam in fresh river water. He ate freshwater fish from the river. He is married and denies sexual contact on the trip. Of the four friends who accompanied him, two also have the same complaint.
retrieved_contexts.Clinical_Findings: The patient is afebrile and organ system examination is normal. On his right upper deltoid is a firm mass with clear margins 38cm in size. On further questioning this mass has recently migrated across his upper chest wall, and a serpiginous tract is visible (Fig. 6.1). There is no additional rash and no lymphadenopathy.
retrieved_contexts.Discussion: A 36-year-old European presents because of a mobile migratory mass he has been noticing for the past 3 weeks. Five weeks ago, he returned from a fishing trip to the Okavango Delta. Two of his travel companions have the same symptoms. Full blood count shows eosinophilia.

retrieved_contexts.Title: A 43-Year-Old Male Traveller Returning from Mozambique With Fever and Eosinophilia
retrieved_contexts.History: A 43-year-old German man presents to a local travel clinic on 21 May because of fever. He had been in Mozambique from 16 April to 30 April, and travelled to Chile afterwards from 30 April to 17 May. He did not take any malaria chemoprophylaxis in Mozambique and reports self-treatment for malaria with atovaquone/proguanil because of fever (27 April to 29 April). He is now complaining of recurrent fever for the past 3 days. The day before presentation his temperature was as high as 39.8°C (103.6°F). He also has some headache and diarrhoea. He reports freshwater contact in a small lake near Maputo. His past medical history is unremarkable.
retrieved_contexts.Clinical_Findings: 43-year-old male, febrile, with a temperature of 39.2°C (102.6°F). The rest of the physical examination is normal and there is no rash, no hepatomegaly, no splenomegaly and no lymphadenopathy.
retrieved_contexts.Discussion: A 43-year-old man presents with of a 3-day history of high fever. He has recently returned from a 5-week trip to Mozambique and Chile. He did not take any malarial chemoprophylaxis, but he took standby emergency treatment for presumed malaria when feeling febrile about 3 weeks ago. He reports freshwater contact in Mozambique. On examination he is febrile. His FBC shows eosinophilia with a normal total white cell count. His liver enzymes, lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) and C-reactive protein (CRP) are slightly raised. Chest radiographyandCTshowsmall,nodularchangesintheperiphery of both lungs.

retrieved_contexts.Title: A 53-Year-Old Man from Malawi With a Chronic Cough
retrieved_contexts.History: A 53-year-old Malawian man presents to a local hospital with a productive cough and whitish sputum for 3 months. He also reports night sweats and some weight loss, which he is unable to quantify. Two months earlier he presented to a health centre with the same complaints. He was given presumptive antimalarials and amoxicillin for 5 days, but to no avail. The patient is not aware of any tuberculosis (TB) contacts. He is currently not on any medication and his past medical history is unremarkable. He is a subsistence farmer. He has never worked in a mine or in the construction industry. He is a non-smoker. He is married with five children; all are well.
retrieved_contexts.Clinical_Findings: 53-year-old man, slightly wasted. Temperature 38.8°C (101.8°F), blood pressure 100/80mmHg, pulse 88bpm, oxygen saturation 97% on ambient air. He appears mildly anaemic. On inspection of his mouth there is no oral thrush, no Kaposi’s sarcoma and no oral hairy leukoplakia. His chest is clear and there are normal heart sounds without any murmurs. There is no lymphadenopathy; liver and spleen are not enlarged.
retrieved_contexts.Discussion: A 53-year-old Malawian man presents with chronic cough and constitutional symptoms. A course of oral antibiotics did not yield any improvement. The patient is not aware of any TB contacts. On admission he is newly diagnosed with HIV-infection and advanced immunosuppression. His sputum microscopy is negative for acid-fast bacilli (AFB). Chest radiography shows a prominent hilar region but is otherwise normal.

retrieved_contexts.Title: A 71-Year-Old Man from Japan With Eosinophilia and a Nodular Lesion in the Lung
retrieved_contexts.History: A 71-year-old Japanese man is referred to a local tertiary care hospital for further work-up of a nodular lesion in his right lung. He is clinically well and does not report any complaints. The lesion was first detected 2 years earlier during a routine healthcheck.Initiallyitwasoflinearshape.Thepatienthasbeen regularly followed up since then. At his most recent follow-up visititwasfoundbychestradiography(Fig.71.1A)andCTscan (Fig. 71.1B, C) that his linear lung shadow had turned into a nodular lesion of about 2cm in diameter. The patient was born in Kyushu district, southern Japan, where he is still living. He has no history of travelling overseas.
retrieved_contexts.Clinical_Findings: The vital signs were normal. The chest was clear. The remainder of the physical examination was also normal.
retrieved_contexts.Discussion: A 71-year-old Japanese man who is clinically well is worked up for a nodular lesion in his right lung. Blood tests reveal a mild eosinophilia and a slightly raised IgE. On PET scan the pulmonary lesion shows an increased FDG uptake.

retrieved_contexts.Title: A 55-Year-Old Couple Both Returning from Chile and Argentina With Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome
retrieved_contexts.History: A 55-year-old Swiss couple, both fitness instructors, travelled for 3 months from Ecuador to Chile. The last month of their trip they spent hiking, camping and taking occasional mud baths in the Chile-Argentinian border region. On their flight back to Switzerland, the husband developed a fever (39°C, 102.2°F), myalgias and generalized weakness that did not respond to symptomatic treatment. At presentation at the hospital in Switzerland 4 days later, he continued to be febrile and felt too weak to walk to the toilet unassisted or even hold up a newspaper. He developed shortness of breath with oxygen desaturation and bilateral interstitial infiltrates were seen on chest x-ray (Fig. 90.1). The respiratory pathogen panel from a nasopharyngeal swab (including influenza A/B, parainfluenza, RSV, adenovirus, rhinovirus, bocavirus, coronavirus and human metapneumovirus) as well as an HIV test came back negative. The following day he was transferred to the intensive care unit for non-invasive ventilator support. Three weeks later, his wife presented with similar complaints and was admitted to the same hospital. She deteriorated rapidly over the 24 hours after admission, developed cardiorespiratory failure and fulfilled fast-entry criteria for extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO). Furthermore, she experienced multi-organ failure requiring hemodialysis, and she developed profuse bleeding from puncture sites in the context of disseminated intravascular coagulation. During the following days, she required mass transfusions of blood products.
retrieved_contexts.Clinical_Findings: Husband: BP 90/55 mmHg, pulse 120 beats per minute, oxygen saturation 94% on ambient air, and temperature 39°C (102.2°F). No abnormal findings on cardiopulmonary auscultation. Wife on admission (3 weeks after her husband’s admission): normal blood pressure, heart rate and oxygen saturation, temperature 38.6°C (101.5°F). No abnormal findings on auscultation.
retrieved_contexts.Discussion: A previously healthy Swiss couple in their mid-50s present with varying degrees of cardiorespiratory failure of 2 and 21 days, respectively, after their return from a 3month trip down the western coast of South America. They spent the last month travelling along the ChileArgentinian border. The cardiorespiratory collapse in the female patient occurs precipitously and requires ECMO treatment.

answer:
Disease: Paracoccidioidomycosis; Reasoning: This is a leading diagnosis. The patient travelled to a highly endemic region (Brazil, Argentina). The clinical presentation of a subacute febrile respiratory illness fits the acute/subacute form of the disease. Most importantly, the chest X-ray findings of nodular and cavitary lesions are characteristic of pulmonary paracoccidioidomycosis. The timeline of symptom onset is also consistent with the typical incubation period. No retrieved cases mention this disease, but the patient's presentation is a textbook example.; Likelihood: high
Disease: Histoplasmosis; Reasoning: Similar to paracoccidioidomycosis, histoplasmosis is an endemic mycosis in South America. Exposure is common in rural areas. The acute form presents as a flu-like illness with pulmonary symptoms. The development of pulmonary nodules is a classic finding. While cavitation is more common in chronic histoplasmosis, it can occur. This diagnosis fits the geographical, clinical, and radiological picture well.; Likelihood: moderate
Disease: Tuberculosis; Reasoning: Tuberculosis is a primary consideration for any patient with cavitary lung lesions and constitutional symptoms like fever. While not specific to his travel destination, the risk of exposure can be increased during travel. The radiological findings are very consistent with post-primary (reactivation) tuberculosis. It is a critical diagnosis to exclude.; Likelihood: moderate
Disease: Hantavirus Cardiopulmonary Syndrome (HCPS); Reasoning: The epidemiology (travel to an endemic region) and initial clinical picture (flu-like prodrome followed by dyspnoea) are highly suggestive of HCPS, as powerfully illustrated by the similarities with Case 90. However, the chest X-ray showing cavitary nodules is strongly atypical for HCPS, which classically causes bilateral interstitial infiltrates and pulmonary edema. The diagnosis is less likely due to this radiological contradiction but cannot be entirely dismissed without serological testing, perhaps as an unusual presentation or a co-infection.; Likelihood: low

question: A 34-year-old man from a high HIV-prevalence area in sub-Saharan Africa presents with a history of recurrent pneumonia. His chest X-ray reveals hilar lymphadenopathy, pleural effusions, and middle/lower lung infiltrates with minimal cavitation. A bronchoscopy confirms the presence of ulcerative mucosa and endobronchial polyps.

Disease: Amebic Liver Abscess with Pleuropulmonary Complications; Reasoning: The diagnosis is almost certain based on a combination of factors:
1. **Epidemiology:** The patient traveled to India, a region highly endemic for *Entamoeba histolytica*.
2. **Clinical Presentation:** The symptoms of right shoulder pain (phrenic nerve irritation from the subphrenic abscess), cough, and radiological evidence of an elevated right hemidiaphragm point directly to a right liver lobe abscess with thoracic extension.
3. **Pathognomonic Findings:** The description of the sputum as "anchovy paste-like" and pleural fluid as "chocolate sauce" is classic for the contents of an amebic abscess, which consists of necrotic hepatocytes rather than true pus. This finding is the single most compelling piece of evidence.
4. **Disease Progression:** This presentation represents a well-described complication of amebic liver abscess, where the abscess erodes through the diaphragm into the pleural space (causing an amebic empyema) and/or the lung parenchyma (forming a hepatobronchial fistula).
5. **Supporting Evidence from Cases:** Case 46 details a patient with a nearly identical demographic and initial symptom profile, confirming that this clinical picture is classic for amebiasis in the region.; Likelihood: high
Disease: Pyogenic Liver Abscess; Reasoning: This is a necessary consideration for any liver abscess. However, several key features argue against it:
1. **Aspirate Character:** Pyogenic abscesses contain purulent, often foul-smelling pus due to bacterial infection. The "anchovy paste" or "chocolate sauce" description is inconsistent with a typical bacterial abscess.
2. **Epidemiology:** While possible anywhere, the specific travel history to India significantly increases the pre-test probability of amebiasis over a pyogenic cause.
3. **Typical Features:** Pyogenic abscesses are often associated with underlying biliary disease or intra-abdominal infections and can be multiple. The presentation here suggests a single, large abscess, which is more characteristic of amebiasis.
No retrieved cases provide support for this diagnosis in this specific clinical context.; Likelihood: low
Disease: Echinococcal (Hydatid) Cyst with Rupture; Reasoning: This is a differential for a cystic liver lesion, especially with travel history.
1. **Aspirate Inconsistency:** The contents of a hydatid cyst are typically clear fluid containing daughter cysts and protoscolices. Rupture or secondary bacterial infection would not result in an "anchovy paste" appearance.
2. **Clinical Course:** Echinococcosis is typically an indolent, slow-growing disease. While rupture can occur, it often leads to anaphylaxis or dissemination, which is not described here. The presentation is more acutely inflammatory than is typical for a hydatid cyst.
3. **Case Comparison:** Case 50 describes a patient with cystic echinococcosis, but the presentation is different, focusing on calcified lesions and biliary obstruction, not pleuropulmonary rupture with this specific type of aspirate.; Likelihood: unlikely

Disease: Strongyloidiasis (Hyperinfection Syndrome); Reasoning: This is the most likely diagnosis. The reasoning is as follows:
1. **Epidemiology:** The patient lived in Southeast Asia, a highly endemic region for *Strongyloides stercoralis*.
2. **Latency:** The parasite's autoinfective life cycle explains the 25-year period between leaving the endemic area and the onset of symptoms. The infection can persist for a lifetime, often asymptomatically.
3. **Clinical Syndrome:** The acute onset of severe pneumonia, bronchospasm, and ARDS is the classic presentation of hyperinfection syndrome, where an uncontrolled proliferation of larvae overwhelms the host, particularly the pulmonary system.
4. **Radiology:** Migrating patchy consolidations are a hallmark of the larval migration through the lung parenchyma, causing inflammation and hemorrhage.
5. **Definitive Evidence:** The isolation of larvae from respiratory samples confirms a diagnosis of pulmonary strongyloidiasis. No retrieved cases described this condition, but the patient's presentation is pathognomonic.; Likelihood: high
Disease: Paragonimiasis; Reasoning: This diagnosis is considered due to the patient's history in Asia and pulmonary involvement, similar to the etiological context of Case 71. Paragonimus (lung fluke) can cause chronic lung disease. However, it is unlikely to be the primary diagnosis because:
1. It does not typically remain latent for decades before causing a fulminant ARDS-like syndrome.
2. The classic presentation is chronic cough, hemoptysis, and cystic or nodular lesions, not acute migrating infiltrates, as seen in the patient and differing from the nodule in Case 71.
3. Diagnosis is typically made by finding characteristic eggs in sputum or stool, not larvae.; Likelihood: unlikely
Disease: Tropical Pulmonary Eosinophilia (TPE); Reasoning: TPE is a hypersensitivity reaction to filarial worms, which are also endemic in Southeast Asia. It can cause cough, bronchospasm, and pulmonary infiltrates. However, it is a poor fit for this patient because:
1. It is an immunological reaction, not a state of overwhelming infection with massive larval dissemination.
2. Larvae are not found in the sputum; the diagnosis relies on clinical signs, extreme eosinophilia, high IgE, and filarial antibodies.
3. It does not typically present as a reactivation after a 25-year asymptomatic period.; Likelihood: unlikely
Disease: Severe Atypical Pneumonia with Bacteremia; Reasoning: A severe bacterial pneumonia could cause ARDS. However, this diagnosis alone does not account for the migrating nature of the infiltrates, the remote travel history as a key feature, or the definitive finding of larvae in respiratory samples. It is important to note, however, that gram-negative bacteremia and meningitis are frequent and often fatal complications of Strongyloides hyperinfection, as migrating larvae can carry enteric bacteria from the gut into the bloodstream and other organs. Therefore, a secondary bacterial infection is highly probable but the primary etiology is parasitic.; Likelihood: low

retrieved_contexts.Title: A 55-Year-Old Couple Both Returning from Chile and Argentina With Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome
retrieved_contexts.History: A 55-year-old Swiss couple, both fitness instructors, travelled for 3 months from Ecuador to Chile. The last month of their trip they spent hiking, camping and taking occasional mud baths in the Chile-Argentinian border region. On their flight back to Switzerland, the husband developed a fever (39°C, 102.2°F), myalgias and generalized weakness that did not respond to symptomatic treatment. At presentation at the hospital in Switzerland 4 days later, he continued to be febrile and felt too weak to walk to the toilet unassisted or even hold up a newspaper. He developed shortness of breath with oxygen desaturation and bilateral interstitial infiltrates were seen on chest x-ray (Fig. 90.1). The respiratory pathogen panel from a nasopharyngeal swab (including influenza A/B, parainfluenza, RSV, adenovirus, rhinovirus, bocavirus, coronavirus and human metapneumovirus) as well as an HIV test came back negative. The following day he was transferred to the intensive care unit for non-invasive ventilator support. Three weeks later, his wife presented with similar complaints and was admitted to the same hospital. She deteriorated rapidly over the 24 hours after admission, developed cardiorespiratory failure and fulfilled fast-entry criteria for extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO). Furthermore, she experienced multi-organ failure requiring hemodialysis, and she developed profuse bleeding from puncture sites in the context of disseminated intravascular coagulation. During the following days, she required mass transfusions of blood products.

No abnormal findings on auscultation.
retrieved_contexts.Discussion: A previously healthy Swiss couple in their mid-50s present with varying degrees of cardiorespiratory failure of 2 and 21 days, respectively, after their return from a 3month trip down the western coast of South America. They spent the last month travelling along the ChileArgentinian border. The cardiorespiratory collapse in the female patient occurs precipitously and requires ECMO treatment.

2. **Clinical Presentation:** The acute onset of high fever, headache, myalgia, and cough is the classic presentation of acute Q fever.
3. **Radiology:** The finding of pneumonia with multiple round opacities and lower lobe infiltrates is a hallmark of Q fever pneumonia.

His HIV status is unknown.

Disease: Brucellosis; Reasoning: The patient's profile fits the classic description for Brucellosis almost perfectly. Key supporting points are: 1) High-risk occupation (slaughterhouse worker) providing direct exposure to infected animals or their products. 2) Geographic location (Mediterranean region) where Brucellosis is endemic. 3) Clinical syndrome of fever, chills, aches/pains (arthralgia/myalgia), and weakness, often termed an 'undulant fever'. Pulmonary involvement can occur but is not always prominent. The diagnosis in Case 76, a patient from the same region with a febrile illness, strongly supports considering Brucellosis. A normal chest radiograph despite a cough is a hallmark feature of Q fever presenting as atypical pneumonia. Distinguishing it from Brucellosis clinically is very difficult, and diagnosis also relies on serology. No retrieved cases are relevant.; Likelihood: high

The constitutional symptoms of fever and weakness are consistent with TB. The most compelling evidence is the bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy seen on the provided chest X-ray, which is a classic finding in primary TB. The mild cough is also a compatible symptom. However, the strong and specific occupational risk for Brucellosis and Q fever makes them slightly more likely initial diagnoses. None of the retrieved cases on TB (33, 11) match this specific clinical presentation of a primary infection.; Likelihood: moderate
Disease: Leptospirosis; Reasoning: Leptospirosis is a zoonosis transmitted via contact with infected animal urine or contaminated environments. While slaughterhouse work is a risk factor, the presentation often includes more specific signs not mentioned here, such as conjunctival suffusion, severe myalgia (especially in calves), headache, and potential progression to severe disease with jaundice and renal failure (Weil's disease). Disease: Leptospirosis (Weil's disease with Severe Pulmonary Hemorrhage Syndrome); Reasoning: This diagnosis is the most likely. The patient's presentation aligns perfectly with severe leptospirosis. 
1. **Epidemiology:** Direct exposure to contaminated freshwater after heavy rain is the classic transmission route for Leptospira bacteria. 
2. **Initial Symptoms:** The prodrome of fever, myalgias, and conjunctival suffusion is textbook for the first phase of leptospirosis. 
3. **Severe Manifestations:** The progression to the icteric triad of intense jaundice, hemorrhage (specifically massive hemoptysis, a hallmark of Severe Pulmonary Hemorrhage Syndrome - SPHS, a devastating complication), and multi-organ failure (respiratory failure) is characteristic of Weil's disease.

However, the combination of intense jaundice and massive hemoptysis makes this less likely than leptospirosis. While liver involvement can occur, severe jaundice is not a typical feature. Respiratory failure is usually due to severe plasma leakage leading to ARDS or pleural effusions, rather than primary pulmonary hemorrhage. No retrieved cases support this diagnosis over leptospirosis.; Likelihood: moderate

While severe, the classic presentation involves hematemesis and renal failure more prominently than massive hemoptysis and respiratory failure. Disease: Disseminated Cryptococcosis; Reasoning: This is the most likely diagnosis. The patient's occupation provides a direct and significant exposure to bird droppings, a classic source of *Cryptococcus neoformans*. The clinical syndrome of prolonged pneumonia and a lymphocyte-predominant pleural effusion is consistent with pulmonary cryptococcosis. The diagnosis being confirmed by 'serologic testing' strongly suggests a cryptococcal antigen (CrAg) test, which is a standard and highly reliable method. Most importantly, if the provided images of skin lesions belong to the patient, the umbilicated papules are a hallmark of disseminated cryptococcosis, which would also explain the severity of the illness and suggest an underlying immunodeficiency.; Likelihood: high
Disease: Progressive Disseminated Histoplasmosis; Reasoning: This is a strong alternative diagnosis. The exposure to bird droppings is also a primary risk factor for *Histoplasma capsulatum*. The pulmonary syndrome, including prolonged cough, fever, and potential for pleural effusion, is nearly identical to cryptococcosis. Diagnosis is also commonly made using serological methods (antigen or antibody tests). The main factor making this slightly less likely than cryptococcosis is that the specific skin lesions (umbilicated papules) are more classic for cryptococcosis, and while histoplasmosis is endemic in the US, it is less common in Southern California than in the Ohio and Mississippi River valleys.; Likelihood: moderate
Disease: Tuberculosis; Reasoning: Tuberculosis is a crucial differential for any patient with prolonged cough, fever, and a lymphocyte-predominant exudative pleural effusion, as exemplified by Case 33. However, two key pieces of evidence argue against it being the final diagnosis in this case. First, there is no epidemiological link to bird droppings. Second, the statement that the diagnosis was confirmed by 'serologic testing' is inconsistent with standard diagnostic practice for active TB, which relies on sputum/fluid culture or nucleic acid amplification tests (NAAT). TB serology is not recommended due to poor accuracy.; Likelihood: low
Disease: Pneumocystis Pneumonia (PCP); Reasoning: While PCP, as seen in Case 23, is a common cause of pneumonia in immunocompromised individuals, it does not fit this patient's profile well. There is no known association with bird dropping exposure. Furthermore, pleural effusions are exceptionally rare in PCP, and diagnosis is made by microscopic identification of organisms in BAL fluid, not typically by serology.; Likelihood: unlikely

2. **Clinical Symptoms:** The parasites attach to the mucosa of the larynx, trachea, or bronchi, causing local inflammation, irritation, and partial obstruction, which perfectly explains the patient's chronic cough, wheezing, pleuritic pain, and hemoptysis.
3. **Epidemiology:** Human syngamosis is a rare zoonosis, but reported cases frequently have a history of travel to or residence in tropical regions, including Southeast Asia (Thailand). Humans are accidental hosts, likely infected by ingesting contaminated food or water.; Likelihood: high

However, it is much less likely given the specific findings. The adult flukes of *Paragonimus* species typically encyst within the lung parenchyma, not the major airways. The patient's bronchoscopy findings are inconsistent with typical paragonimiasis.; Likelihood: low

The bronchoscopic finding of macroscopic worms attached to the airway mucosa effectively rules out strongyloidiasis as the cause of this specific finding.; Likelihood: unlikely
